case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Oklahoma may constitutionally exclude St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School from the state charter-school program because of its religious character, given the Religion Clauses and the threshold question whether the charter school is a state actor.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Exercise Clause and Establishment Clause); Oklahoma Charter Schools Act, Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134 (B)(1-35) (as referenced in the materials).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (the Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board and St. Isidore) argue that Oklahoma’s categorical exclusion of a charter school based on religious status/character violates the Free Exercise Clause under the Court’s recent funding-and-private-choice cases. They contend the charter-school program involves parental private choice (analogous to neutral benefit programs), and that state oversight/contractual regulation does not transform the school into the State itself. They also suggest the Oklahoma Supreme Court overstated 'entwinement' and misapplied state-action doctrine, with Rendell-Baker offered as the closest factual analogy supporting the view that heavy public funding/regulation does not automatically make a private school a state actor.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Oklahoma Attorney General) maintains that St. Isidore would operate as a public/charter school carrying out a governmental education function under substantial state control and oversight, making it a state actor whose religious evangelizing would be attributable to the State. On that view, approving a sectarian charter would amount to the State creating or operating a religious public school—impermissible under the Establishment Clause—and thus Oklahoma may (or must) exclude it. Respondent also argues there is no relevant circuit split because the Oklahoma Supreme Court applied standard state-action frameworks (including entwinement/public function) to find sufficient governmental control and attribution.
key_precedents: Brentwood Academy v. Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Ass’n, 531 U.S. 288 (2001)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas fairly press that Rendell-Baker rejects treating funding and ordinary oversight as enough for state action, and that Zelman/Carson caution against using Establishment “avoidance” to justify religious exclusions in neutral-aid programs. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, Oklahoma has not simply subsidized private schooling; it has statutorily constituted charter schools as a tuition-free part of the State’s public-school system with continuing authorization, renewal, and revocation powers that integrate the operator into the State’s own educational apparatus in a way that is closer to Brentwood’s entwinement than to an arm’s-length contractor relationship. Once the provision of instruction is fairly attributable to the State, the private-choice framework of Zelman is a mismatch, because the State is not facilitating private choices so much as delegating operation of a “public school.” On narrow grounds that preserve institutional legitimacy, I would hold only that a State may insist its own public schools (including those it defines and administers as such) remain nonsectarian, without extending Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson to compel the State to operate a religious public school.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Oklahoma’s statutory decision to call charters “public schools,” combined with authorization/renewal/revocation, creates Brentwood-style “entwinement” such that the school’s instruction becomes state action. But under a textualist/originalist approach, state-action attribution cannot rise or fall on legislative labels or generalized supervisory leverage; Rendell-Baker remains the closer analogue because the State does not direct the specific challenged conduct (religious instruction and governance), and Brentwood involved identity-level intermixture with public officials that is not present here. Justice Alito’s Establishment-avoidance rationale depends on first treating the religious instruction as the State’s own operation; absent that attribution, excluding St. Isidore because it is religious is discrimination in a generally available charter framework prohibited by Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson, with Zelman confirming that neutral participation does not itself establish religion. I therefore see no argument presented that genuinely undermines the core premise that the relevant religious decisions remain private conduct not fairly attributable to the State.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is that Rendell-Baker warns against treating funding, regulation, and statutory “public” labels as dispositive, and that Brentwood entwinement requires more than ordinary oversight. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Oklahoma has not merely purchased services from a private school; it has made charters a tuition-free component of the State’s public-school system, with ongoing authorization, renewal, and revocation that functionally delegates the State’s obligation to provide public education—making the instructional enterprise fairly attributable to the State in a way Rendell-Baker’s arms-length contractor was not. Once the State-action attribution is accepted, Carson/Zelman’s private-choice logic is a mismatch because the State is not neutrally subsidizing private options; it is constituting and operating (through delegation) a public school, and the practical consequence of compelling a sectarian “public school” raises serious Establishment Clause concerns the State may avoid. Under my approach, Oklahoma can draw a clear nonsectarian line for institutions it chooses to treat as public schools without thereby discriminating against private religious exercise in a general aid program.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—echoed by Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett—is that Rendell-Baker cautions against finding state action from funding and regulation absent control over the challenged religious conduct, and that Zelman/Carson’s private-choice logic limits Establishment Clause “avoidance.” But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan correctly reframe the threshold: Oklahoma has not merely purchased services from a private school; it has statutorily integrated charter schools into its tuition-free public-school system with authorization, renewal, and revocation powers that make the delivery of instruction an exercise of delegated state function and, under Brentwood’s entwinement framework, fairly attributable to the State. Once the State has chosen this structural model, the relevant constitutional harm is not “aid following private choice” but the State operating—through a public instrumentality—a sectarian public school, a real-world Establishment Clause concern Oklahoma may avoid without extending Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson to compel religious operation of the State’s own schools. Under a pragmatic approach attentive to vulnerable students and families, a clear nonsectarian boundary in the State’s public-school apparatus protects equal access and prevents coercive religious sorting within a government school setting.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh make the strongest point that Rendell-Baker cautions against treating funding and regulation as dispositive and that Brentwood involved deeper governance intermixture; I agree labels alone cannot do the work. But Oklahoma’s statutory design does more than label: it constitutes charters as tuition-free public schools within the State system, funds them as public schools through State Aid, and retains continuing authorization/renewal/revocation authority that integrates the operator’s core instructional function into the State’s educational apparatus—bringing this closer to Brentwood’s “entwinement” than to an arms-length contractor. Once the school’s operation is fairly attributable to the State, Zelman/Carson’s private-choice framework (which Justice Thomas emphasizes) is a mismatch because the challenged conduct is not aid to private choice but the State’s delegated operation of its own public school, and the State may insist that public schools it runs remain nonsectarian. Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson therefore do not compel a right to operate a sectarian public instrumentality, because those cases addressed exclusion from generally available benefits to private parties, not the composition and governance of the State’s own school system.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Brentwood entwinement theory is the strongest point for Respondents, but it still treats statutory “public school” labeling plus authorization/renewal/revocation as enough to convert a private operator’s religious governance into state action. Brentwood turned on identity-level intermixture—public officials effectively constituting and running the association—whereas this record looks closer to Rendell-Baker: substantial funding and oversight without state direction of the specific challenged conduct (religious instruction and governance). Once the religious decisions are not fairly attributable to Oklahoma, the State’s categorical exclusion triggers Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson, and the Establishment-Clause “avoidance” concern loses force under Zelman because neutral participation does not make the State the speaker. Justice Sotomayor’s “public-school function” framing does not alter the analysis because education has not been treated in our precedents as a traditionally exclusive public function that alone transforms contractors into the State.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Oklahoma has integrated charters into its public-school system—labeling them “public schools” and retaining authorization/renewal/revocation—so sectarian instruction is fairly attributable to the State under Brentwood. But Brentwood’s entwinement turned on governance- and identity-level intermixture with public officials, and Rendell-Baker remains the closer fit: pervasive funding and regulation, plus a state-created framework, do not by themselves make a private operator’s curricular/religious decisions state action absent meaningful state control over the challenged conduct. I also agree with Justice Gorsuch that Zelman/Carson weaken the “Establishment avoidance” rationale once the religious instruction is not attributable to the State; without that attribution, Oklahoma’s categorical exclusion looks like disqualifying a religious provider from an otherwise generally available charter benefit. Oklahoma can police performance, nondiscrimination, and public accountability, but on this record it cannot impose a flat nonsectarian condition that targets religious status/use without first satisfying our state-action precedents.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s entwinement point is the strongest for Respondents, but Brentwood’s “pervasive entwinement” turned on governance-level intermixture and institutional identity, not simply a State’s decision to call something “public” and regulate it; Rendell-Baker remains the closer fit because Oklahoma has not been shown to control or direct the specific challenged religious instruction or governance. Justice Alito’s Establishment-avoidance rationale depends on first attributing the sectarian teaching to the State, and under our state-action doctrine that attribution cannot be bootstrapped from statutory labels and leverage that stop short of control over the challenged conduct. Zelman and our Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson line reinforce that, absent state action as to the religious instruction itself, a categorical religious disqualification in an otherwise generally available program is presumptively unconstitutional discrimination. I therefore stay with Petitioners: Oklahoma may enforce neutral performance and operational requirements, but it cannot exclude on religious status/use without a stronger showing that the religious instruction is fairly attributable to the State under Brentwood rather than merely funded/regulated under Rendell-Baker.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that Brentwood requires governance-level intermixture and that Rendell-Baker rejects state action from funding/regulation absent control over the specific religious conduct—does not defeat attribution here because Oklahoma has affirmatively constituted charters as tuition-free “public schools” within its own system and retains continuing authorization/renewal/revocation power over the core instructional function, which is more like structural entwinement than an arm’s-length contractor. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively explain why Zelman’s private-choice logic is a poor fit once the State is not merely subsidizing private choice but delegating operation of a public-school instrumentality; the practical consequence is that sectarian instruction would be fairly understood as the State’s own public-school offering. Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson therefore do not compel a right to operate a religious public school, because those cases protect religious participation in neutral aid programs for private actors, not religious control over a State-created public-school slot. On a narrow, administrable rule, Oklahoma may enforce a nonsectarian boundary for entities it defines and operates (through delegation) as public schools without triggering Free Exercise discrimination.

John Roberts.reasoning: Oklahoma’s Charter Schools Act repeatedly defines a charter school as a “public school” formed and operated under state law and funded through the State Aid system, Okla. Stat. tit. 70, §§ 3-132(A), 3-132.2(C)(1), which supports treating St. Isidore as a state actor for First Amendment purposes. Under Brentwood Academy, pervasive entwinement and governmental control can make ostensibly private entities’ actions attributable to the State, and here the program’s structure is closer to a state-created public education instrumentality than the private-contractor arrangement in Rendell-Baker. If the school’s religious instruction is state action, authorizing it would risk the State’s operation of a religious public school, raising serious Establishment Clause concerns that counsel a narrow resolution on state-action grounds rather than extending Zelman/Carson (which involved neutral aid and private choice among private schools). Given those institutional and federalism interests, Oklahoma may exclude a sectarian charter from its public-school system without violating the Free Exercise Clause.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Oklahoma’s categorical exclusion of St. Isidore because of its religious character violates the Free Exercise Clause: once the State creates a generally available benefit program, it may not disqualify otherwise eligible participants based on religious status or use. Carson v. Makin, 596 U.S. 767 (2022). The threshold state-action theory is not satisfied merely because the school is publicly funded and regulated; under Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, 457 U.S. 830, 840–42 (1982), extensive public funding and oversight do not transform a private operator into the State, and education is not a function “traditionally the exclusive prerogative” of the State. Because the program operates through parental choice akin to Zelman v. Simmons-Harris, 536 U.S. 639 (2002), any religious instruction is attributable to private choice rather than state establishment, and Oklahoma cannot invoke the Establishment Clause to impose a religious disability.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Oklahoma’s charter-school program, by text and design, creates and funds “public school[s]” under substantial state control and supervision, Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134, so a charter’s operation is best understood as governmental action rather than merely a neutral benefit to private actors. Under Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA, the degree of governmental involvement and institutional integration supports attributing the school’s conduct to the State; and if the school’s religious instruction is state-attributable, approving it would effectively establish a sectarian public school in tension with the Establishment Clause. Rendell-Baker v. Kohn does not compel a contrary result because it addressed a private contractor’s employment decision and emphasized that funding and regulation alone are insufficient, whereas here the State is authorizing an entity to operate as a public school within the State’s own system. Given the practical consequences of treating charter schools as private for Religion Clause purposes—inviting state-sponsored religious schooling—Oklahoma may constitutionally exclude St. Isidore based on its religious character.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Oklahoma may exclude St. Isidore because a charter school created under the Oklahoma Charter Schools Act, Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134, operates as part of the State’s public-school system under extensive state authorization, oversight, and renewal/revocation power—making its operation attributable to the State under the entwinement framework of Brentwood Academy v. Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Ass’n. If the school is a state actor, authorizing it to provide religious instruction and evangelize would effectively make Oklahoma responsible for operating a sectarian public school, raising a direct Establishment Clause problem the State is entitled (and may be compelled) to avoid under U.S. Const. amend. I. Petitioners’ reliance on private-choice funding cases like Carson v. Makin and Zelman is misplaced because this program is not a neutral benefit delivered to families who independently select among private providers; it is the State’s delegation of a core public education function to an entity that would still be operating “as” a public school. Rendell-Baker v. Kohn does not control because that case involved a privately run school not created as a public school and lacked the same governmental integration and policy/management entwinement present in a state charter framework.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Oklahoma’s Charter Schools Act authorizes only “public schools” and integrates charter schools into the State’s public-education system, see Okla. Stat. tit. 70, §§ 3-132(A), 3-132.2(C)(1), with full public funding and pervasive oversight—features that make the school’s provision of instruction fairly attributable to the State under the “entwinement” framework of Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA. That state-action conclusion distinguishes this case from Rendell-Baker, where a privately run school—even if heavily funded and regulated—was not deemed the State itself, because Oklahoma has statutorily designated and structured charters as public institutions rather than contractors. If the charter is a state actor, then authorizing a school that intends to provide religious instruction and evangelization would risk attributing religious exercise to the State, implicating the Establishment Clause in a way the private-choice funding cases (Zelman; Carson) do not. On this record, Oklahoma may constitutionally insist that the public-school program it creates and operates remain nonsectarian, without triggering Free Exercise invalidation based on status discrimination.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Oklahoma’s Charter Schools Act defines charter schools as “public school[s],” Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-132(D), but labels do not resolve the federal constitutional question of state action; the State must show the school’s challenged religious decisions are fairly attributable to it under settled doctrine. Under Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, heavy public funding and pervasive regulation of a school do not, without more, convert a privately operated school into a state actor, and education is not a “traditionally exclusive prerogative” of the State. If St. Isidore is not a state actor, then Oklahoma’s categorical exclusion based on religious character triggers the Free Exercise rule of Trinity Lutheran/Espinoza/Carson and is unconstitutional because the program distributes a generally available benefit in a neutral, choice-based manner. And even assuming heightened oversight, Zelman confirms that neutral aid reaching religious schools through private choice does not violate the Establishment Clause, so the State’s asserted Establishment interest cannot justify religious-status discrimination.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Oklahoma’s categorical exclusion of St. Isidore from the charter-school program because of its religious character triggers this Court’s Free Exercise precedents barring status- or use-based disqualification from generally available public benefits, see Carson v. Makin, 596 U.S. 767 (2022), and the program’s structure resembles neutral funding mediated by family choice rather than direct State religious operation, cf. Zelman v. Simmons-Harris, 536 U.S. 639 (2002). The threshold state-action determination is not satisfied merely by public funding and extensive regulation; under Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, 457 U.S. 830, 840–842 (1982), such features do not transform a privately run school into the State, and operating a tuition-free school is not a “traditional, exclusive” public function in the state-action sense. Nor does the level of oversight described, without day-to-day governmental control, establish the kind of pervasive entwinement required by Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA, 531 U.S. 288, 296 (2001). Given those limits, Oklahoma’s reliance on an Establishment Clause avoidance theory is insufficient to justify a blanket exclusion under Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134(B) when the program otherwise permits private operators and is administered on neutral criteria.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Oklahoma’s categorical exclusion of St. Isidore because of its religious character is presumptively unconstitutional under the Free Exercise Clause as construed in Carson v. Makin, which forbids denying generally available public benefits on account of religious status or religious use. The threshold question is state action, and under Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, extensive public funding and detailed regulation of a school do not, without more, convert a privately operated school into the State; education is not a function that has been “traditionally the exclusive prerogative” of government. Although Oklahoma law defines a “charter school” as a “public school,” Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-132(D), that label cannot by itself resolve the federal constitutional attribution inquiry, and the program’s structure—providing schooling through contracted operators chosen by parents—resembles neutral private-choice arrangements approved in Zelman v. Simmons-Harris. Because the school is best understood as a private contractor participating in a neutral program rather than the State itself, Oklahoma may not bar participation solely due to religious character.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the Oklahoma Charter Schools Act, Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134, a charter school is created by the State to deliver a tuition-free public education under ongoing governmental authorization and oversight; on this record, that level of state creation, supervision, and integration supports treating the operator as a state actor under Brentwood Academy v. TSSAA. If the school is a state actor, approving a sectarian charter would risk attributing religious instruction to the State itself, raising serious Establishment Clause concerns that are not cured merely by families’ enrollment decisions (distinguishing Zelman’s private-choice aid program). Rendell-Baker does not compel the opposite result because it involved a private school whose employment decisions were not fairly attributable to the State, whereas here the charter program structures the school as part of the State’s public-school system. Given those practical consequences and the need for clear procedural boundaries between public education and religious exercise, Oklahoma may constitutionally exclude St. Isidore from operating as a public charter school.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Oklahoma may, consistent with the First Amendment’s Religion Clauses, exclude St. Isidore from the state charter-school program because it is religious (and relatedly whether a charter school is a state actor such that operating a sectarian charter school would be state-sponsored religion).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, First Amendment (Free Exercise Clause and Establishment Clause); Oklahoma Charter Schools Act (Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134); and (as applied by the Oklahoma Supreme Court) the Oklahoma Constitution’s limits on state support of religion.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (the Charter School Board and St. Isidore) argue that excluding a school from generally available charter-school participation solely because of its religious character is unconstitutional religious discrimination under the Free Exercise Clause; they emphasize private choice (families choose to enroll), analogize to the Supreme Court’s recent Free Exercise decisions involving equal access to public benefits, and contend the State’s oversight/regulation of charter schools does not convert the school’s religious instruction into state action or an Establishment Clause violation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Oklahoma AG) argues Oklahoma’s charter schools are public schools and/or state actors whose actions are fairly attributable to the State due to extensive governmental creation, funding, and operational oversight (entwinement/public-function); therefore authorizing a sectarian charter school would amount to the State establishing or sponsoring religion, and Oklahoma may (or must) bar religious charter schools to comply with the Establishment Clause and state constitutional restrictions.
key_precedents: Brentwood Acad. v. Tenn. Secondary Sch. Athletic Ass’n, 531 U.S. 288 (2001)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press Rendell-Baker’s warning that funding, regulation, and labels do not automatically create state action, and that Free Exercise ordinarily forbids excluding a participant based on religious status. But as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan emphasize, this scheme goes beyond arm’s-length contracting: Oklahoma has by statute constituted charters as "public schools" within its own system, tasked them with delivering the State’s public-education obligation, and retained continuing supervisory and revocation authority—features that make the challenged conduct (running a tuition-free public school with sectarian instruction) fairly attributable to the State under Brentwood’s entwinement/public-function logic. Once attribution is established, the State’s interest is not mere hostility to religion but avoiding the State itself operating a religious public school—something Zelman/Carson’s private-choice framework does not resolve. On minimalist grounds, we can decide only that where a State structures charters as state instrumentalities in its public-school system, it may insist on nonsectarian instruction without triggering the equal-access rule applicable to genuinely private beneficiaries.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest point—that Oklahoma’s statutory designation of charters as “public schools” performing a core educational function, plus renewal/revocation oversight, creates Brentwood-style entwinement and thus state attribution of religious instruction. But Brentwood requires genuine structural interpenetration of public officials and decisionmaking; a State’s choice to fund, regulate, and retain termination authority over a contractor does not, without more, make the contractor’s religious curriculum the State’s own speech or act, and Rendell-Baker remains the closer fit because the challenged conduct (religious instruction) is not shown to be compelled or dictated by the State. Labels cannot do the constitutional work: the State may not convert private actors into “state actors” simply by calling them public, then invoke its own relabeling to justify excluding religious participants from a generally available program. Because the exclusion turns on the school’s religious character and not on any state-directed religious activity, the Free Exercise violation is clear and the Establishment Clause does not require this discrimination.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is Rendell-Baker: funding and regulation, even extensive, do not by themselves make a private school’s decisions state action, and Free Exercise bars exclusion from generally available benefits based on religious status. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, Oklahoma has not merely subsidized private education; it has statutorily constituted charter schools as “public schools” to discharge the State’s own constitutional duty, under ongoing supervisory and revocation authority—features that move this case toward Brentwood’s entwinement/public-function analysis rather than Rendell-Baker’s arm’s-length contractor model. Once the State has created and integrated the entity into its public-school system, sectarian instruction is fairly attributable to the State, and Oklahoma may insist on nonsectarian operation to avoid the practical and constitutional consequences of state-sponsored religious education. Zelman/Carson’s private-choice rationale does not translate cleanly where the State is authorizing a religious public school as part of its own compulsory public program, so I remain with Respondent on a narrow, administrable ground.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Rendell-Baker point is the best for Petitioner, but it doesn’t grapple with the particular conduct and structure here: Oklahoma has created charter schools as “public schools” within its own compulsory, tuition-free system and empowered an authorizer with continuing supervisory and revocation authority, making sectarian instruction plausibly attributable to the State under Brentwood-style entwinement. Unlike Rendell-Baker’s arm’s-length contractor and personnel-decision context, the State here is delegating and supervising performance of its core constitutional duty to provide public education, so the Establishment Clause avoidance interest is not speculative but immediate for religious minorities and nonadherents. As Chief Justice Roberts urges, we can decide narrowly that when a State designs charters as instrumentalities of its public-school system, it may insist on religious neutrality without triggering Carson/Zelman’s equal-access rule for private-choice subsidies. Free Exercise is weighty, but it does not require the State itself to operate (or be seen to operate) a religious public school program.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Rendell-Baker point is the hardest: funding, regulation, and even contracting do not automatically convert a private operator into the State, and Free Exercise bars religion-based exclusion from generally available benefits. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that this statute does more than subsidize private choice—it constitutes charters as “public schools” within the State’s own system and subjects them to continuing authorizer renewal/revocation control, which looks like Brentwood-style entwinement and delegation of the State’s core education function rather than an arm’s-length contractor relationship. Once the specific conduct at issue—operating a tuition-free public school as part of the State’s school system—is fairly attributable to the State, Oklahoma has a substantial Establishment-Clause-avoidance interest that Zelman/Carson (private-choice aid to private schools) do not resolve. A narrow holding keyed to state-action attribution and the State’s own structural design, as Roberts proposes, is the most coherent and administrable way to reconcile the Religion Clauses here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press Rendell-Baker’s warning that funding and regulation, standing alone, do not convert a private operator into the State, and that statutory labels cannot do all the work. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Oklahoma has done more than subsidize or contract: it has by law constituted charter schools as “public schools” within the State’s own free public-education system, coupled with continuing sponsor supervision and revocation authority, making this a delegated public function with Brentwood-style entwinement rather than an arm’s-length private benefit program. That structural integration means the specific conduct at issue—running a tuition-free public school as part of the State system—is fairly attributable to the State, so the State may insist on nonsectarian operation to avoid state-sponsored religious instruction. Zelman and Carson therefore do not control, because they involved private choice among private schools, not the State authorizing a religious public school within its own governmental apparatus.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Rendell-Baker point is the strongest for Petitioner, but it does not control where the State has statutorily constituted the entity as a “public school” within its own system and retained continuing renewal/revocation authority; that looks less like arm’s-length contracting and more like Brentwood-style entwinement/public-function delegation. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, this is not a Zelman/Carson private-choice benefit program but the State’s own delivery mechanism for public education, so sectarian instruction is fairly attributable to the State and triggers a serious Establishment Clause avoidance interest. Under an institutionalist, administrable approach, a narrow holding tied to state-action attribution and the historic tradition of nonsectarian public schools avoids forcing States either to sponsor religious public schools or to dismantle charter regimes. I therefore remain with Respondent because Thomas’s framework understates the statutory integration and practical consequences that make this program meaningfully different from Rendell-Baker and the equal-access cases.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press Rendell-Baker’s warning that funding, regulation, and statutory labels do not alone create state action, but that framing elides what Oklahoma has done here: it has constituted charter schools by law as "public schools" within its own system and empowered an authorizer with renewal/revocation authority to supervise their operation, which is closer to Brentwood’s entwinement than arm’s-length contracting. Chief Justice Roberts’s distinction from Zelman/Carson is persuasive under a textualist approach because those cases involve private choice among private providers, while this program would place sectarian instruction inside the State’s own public-school apparatus, making the religious teaching fairly attributable to the State. On that attribution, Oklahoma’s exclusion is not discrimination against a private beneficiary but a limitation on what the State itself may do in its public-education program, and Establishment-Clause-avoidance is a sufficient justification. Rendell-Baker therefore does not undermine my conclusion because the relevant “specific conduct” here is the operation of a tuition-free public school under ongoing state supervisory control, not a private school’s independent internal decisions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Rendell-Baker point is the best argument for Petitioner, but it assumes this is arm’s-length contracting with a private school; here, as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Oklahoma has statutorily constituted charter schools as “public schools” within the State’s own system to discharge a constitutional duty, with continuing renewal/revocation authority that makes the educational program fairly attributable to the State. That structural integration fits Brentwood’s entwinement/public-function logic more than Rendell-Baker’s posture, so the challenged conduct is not merely a private recipient’s religious use of funds but state-sponsored religious instruction in a public school. Carson/Zelman therefore do not control because they involved private choice among private providers, whereas this program risks coercion and unequal treatment inside a compulsory, publicly administered institution. On my pragmatic, procedural-fairness approach, Oklahoma may exclude sectarian charter schools to avoid Establishment Clause attribution without converting this into a Free Exercise “equal access” mandate.

John Roberts.reasoning: Oklahoma’s charter schools are created by state law and operated as part of the State’s public-school system under the Oklahoma Charter Schools Act (Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134 et seq.), with public funding and continuing supervisory control, so authorizing a sectarian charter risks attributing religious instruction to the State under an entwinement/public-function analysis. That posture distinguishes the case from the neutral-aid/private-choice line in Zelman v. Simmons-Harris, 536 U.S. 639 (2002), and from the generally available private-benefit programs in Carson v. Makin, 596 U.S. 767 (2022), because the program here looks less like subsidizing private options and more like the State operating “public schools.” While Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, 457 U.S. 830 (1982), cautions that funding and regulation alone do not create state action, the charter-school context plausibly involves the State delegating the quintessential governmental function of providing a public education, and we should avoid a broad ruling that would force States to treat religious entities as operators of public schools. On narrow grounds protective of institutional legitimacy, the State may exclude sectarian charter schools to avoid an Establishment Clause problem.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause forbids a State from excluding an otherwise eligible participant from a generally available public-benefits program solely because of its religious character, and Oklahoma’s charter-school program is such a benefit program. Oklahoma’s heavy funding and regulation do not, without more, convert a privately operated school into a state actor: in Rendell-Baker v. Kohn, the Court held that a school receiving “virtually all” its income from the government and subject to “extensive and detailed” regulation was not state action. Oklahoma may label charter schools “public schools” in Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-134 and related provisions, but a State cannot evade federal constitutional limits through statutory labels; absent a sufficient nexus or coercive control, authorizing a religious charter school does not itself establish religion. Because the exclusion is religious discrimination and the Establishment Clause does not require it, Oklahoma’s denial violates the Free Exercise Clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Oklahoma’s Charter Schools Act defines a charter school as a “public school,” Okla.
